summary: Arabic often says “when” with no preposition at all: the time word goes into the accusative, the “adverbial accusative” — يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ (on Friday), صَبَاحًا (in the morning), ظُهْرًا (at noon), مَسَاءً (in the evening), لَيْلًا (at night), اللَّيْلَةَ (tonight). The time adverbs are such accusatives too: الْيَوْمَ (today, “the day”), غَدًا (tomorrow), الْآنَ (now), لَاحِقًا (later), قَرِيبًا (soon), مُبَكِّرًا (early), مُتَأَخِّرًا (late), and the frequency words دَائِمًا (always), غَالِبًا (usually), كَثِيرًا (often), أَحْيَانًا (sometimes) — the same -an as in شُكْرًا and مَرْحَبًا. أَمْسِ (yesterday) is the exception: it ends in -i and never changes. Instead of the accusative you may use فِي + genitive (فِي الصَّبَاحِ, فِي يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ) or عِنْدَ for a moment (عِنْدَ الظُّهْرِ). The days are mostly numbers with the article — الْأَحَد “the one”, الِاثْنَيْن “the two”, الثُّلَاثَاء, الْأَرْبِعَاء, الْخَمِيس (three, four, five) — then الْجُمُعَة (the gathering) and السَّبْت (the Sabbath); a day is “day + name”: يَوْمُ الْأَحَدِ. “Today is Sunday” is a verbless sentence: الْيَوْمُ الْأَحَدُ. Time words stand at the start or at the end of the sentence.

blocks.caption: Always with the article; on a day = يَوْمَ + the name in the genitive: يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ.
How often — from always to never.

blocks.title: The adverbial accusative.
blocks.text: An accusative noun can say when: يَوْمَ, صَبَاحًا, مَسَاءً, لَيْلًا — the -an you already know from شُكْرًا, أَهْلًا and مَرْحَبًا. German does it too: eines Tages, jeden Morgen (accusative / genitive of time).

blocks.title: الْيَوْمُ or الْيَوْمَ?
blocks.text: With -a it is the adverb “today”: الْيَوْمَ أَعْمَلُ. With -u it is the subject “the day”: الْيَوْمُ الْأَحَدُ (today is Sunday), الْيَوْمُ يَوْمُ عُطْلَةٍ (today is a holiday).

blocks.title: Today is Monday.
blocks.text: With Monday say الْيَوْمُ يَوْمُ الِاثْنَيْنِ: الِاثْنَيْنِ is an old dual, and after يَوْمُ it keeps the form everyone uses.
Yesterday asks for the past: كُنْتُ فِي الْبَيْتِ أَمْسِ (I was at home yesterday) — the past tense comes in lesson C01; كَانَ (lesson 1) is enough for now.

askYourself: A day of the week? → يَوْمَ + the name (يَوْمَ السَّبْتِ), or فِي يَوْمِ السَّبْتِ; the name always has al-.
A part of the day? → the accusative (صَبَاحًا, مَسَاءً, لَيْلًا, ظُهْرًا) or فِي + al- (فِي الصَّبَاحِ); the afternoon is بَعْدَ الظُّهْرِ.
Today, tomorrow, yesterday, now? → الْيَوْمَ, غَدًا, أَمْسِ, الْآنَ — no preposition.
Saying what day it is? → a verbless sentence: الْيَوْمُ الْأَحَدُ.
How often? → دَائِمًا, غَالِبًا, كَثِيرًا, أَحْيَانًا; never = لَا + verb + أَبَدًا.
Early or late? → مُبَكِّرًا / مُتَأَخِّرًا; later (afterwards) → لَاحِقًا.

traps: *يَوْمُ الْأَحَدِ أَذْهَبُ … → يَوْمَ الْأَحَدِ أَذْهَبُ …: “on” is the accusative -a.
*أَحَدٌ for Sunday → الْأَحَدُ: the day names always have the article.
مَسَاءً has no alif after the tanwīn (it ends in a hamza); صَبَاحًا and لَيْلًا have one.

quiz.why: “On” a day: يَوْمَ (accusative) + the day in the genitive.

quiz.q: “I go to work in the morning.”
quiz.why: The accusative صَبَاحًا is the adverb “in the morning”.
A verbless sentence: subject and predicate in the nominative.
أَحْيَانًا = at times; دَائِمًا always, غَالِبًا usually, لَاحِقًا later.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew numbers the days the same way: יוֹם רִאשׁוֹן, יוֹם שֵׁנִי … (first, second …), then שַׁבָּת = السَّبْت; “in the morning” is בַּבֹּקֶר with בְּ, where Arabic can use the accusative صَبَاحًا.
German: am Montag, am Morgen, heute / morgen / gestern; Arabic: يَوْمَ الِاثْنَيْنِ, صَبَاحًا — an accusative instead of “am”. German also has accusatives of time: jeden Tag = كُلَّ يَوْمٍ.
Chinese numbers the days too: 星期一 … 星期六 (week + one … six), 星期天; time words stand before the verb: 我明天去. Arabic is freer: غَدًا أَذْهَبُ / أَذْهَبُ غَدًا.
